title: API Design: Idempotency Makes APIs Safe

scenes.line1: Why do some API calls repeat safely?
scenes.say: Ever wonder why some API calls can be repeated without causing problems? Let's break down the secret sauce.

scenes.label: Idempotent
scenes.sub: Safe to repeat: GET, PUT, DELETE. POST is not.
scenes.say: The key is idempotency. Actions like get, put, and delete are safe to repeat. Post, though, is not.

rows.b: Replace data, same result every time
Creates new data, repeats can duplicate

scenes.say: Get reads data and never changes things. Put always replaces data, so repeating it does nothing new. Delete removes data, and if you try again, nothing breaks. But post creates new stuff, so repeating it can make duplicates.
Idempotent actions mean you can retry without fear. Not idempotent? You risk duplicates and weird bugs.

scenes.question: Can you safely retry POST requests?
scenes.wrong: Yes, POST is always safe to retry.
scenes.right: No, POST isn't idempotent. Use idempotency keys to avoid duplicates.
scenes.say: A common trap: thinking post is always safe to retry. It's not. You need idempotency keys to make repeated posts safe.
